title: A Chief Buried Under Golden Bulls
text: In a great burial mound in the northwest Caucasus, an important person was laid to rest with eight long gold and silver tubes and little bull figures. Long thought to be canopy poles or sceptres, they may really be straws for sharing beer. Dug up in 1897, the Maikop kurgan is described as the richest burial mound of the Early Bronze Age.

source.name: St Petersburg University news, on Trifonov, Savelieva et al., Antiquity 2022, 'Party like a Sumerian: reinterpreting the sceptres from the Maikop kurgan'

title: The Goddess Temple of Niuheliang
text: In the hills of northeast China, the Hongshan people built stone burial mounds, altars and a 'Goddess Temple' between about 5,500 and 5,000 years ago. Inside the temple were parts of six clay figures with female features, including a life-size head. Graves nearby held only jade, carved into dragons, birds, tortoises and people.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (Tentative List: Sites of Hongshan Culture)

title: The Oldest Picture of a Wagon
text: A clay pot from a farming village in southern Poland is decorated with simple drawings that look like a four-wheeled wagon. It is one of the oldest images of a wheeled vehicle anywhere. Wheels seem to have spread across Europe and the Middle East surprisingly fast, almost as soon as they were invented.

source.name: Archaeological Museum in Kraków, 'Vase from Bronocice'

source2.name: Antiquity 73 (1999), Bakker, Kruk, Lanting & Milisauskas, 'The earliest evidence of wheeled vehicles in Europe and the Near East' (abstract via Crossref)

title: The World's First Swords
text: In a palace complex on a 30-metre-high mound on the Malatya plain, archaeologists found exceptional metal weapons made of copper mixed with arsenic, among them the earliest swords so far known in the world. The rulers seem to have shown them off as signs of their new power. The palace also reveals a sophisticated system of administration that existed before writing.

title: Egypt's First Written Labels
text: Tombs at Abydos that are older than Egypt's First Dynasty held small ivory labels carved with signs, along with pottery and the names of early kings. The inscribed labels show that Egyptian writing had reached an advanced stage earlier than anyone had realised, long before the first pharaohs ruled a united Egypt.

title: Newgrange Catches the Winter Sun
text: Stone Age farmers in Ireland built a huge round mound of stones, about 85 metres across, with a long stone passage inside. Above the entrance is a small 'roof-box'. On mornings around the winter solstice, the shortest day of the year, the rising sun shines through it, along the passage and into the chamber deep inside for a few minutes.

title: Stone Age Homes With Furniture
text: On the windy Orkney Islands, villagers built snug houses linked by covered passages, with beds, shelves and dressers all made of stone. Because trees were scarce, stone furniture was the clever solution. The village lay hidden under sand until a fierce storm in 1850 blew the dunes away.

title: The King Who Wore Two Crowns
text: A carved slate slab from Hierakonpolis shows King Narmer wearing the crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the crown of Lower Egypt on the other. Two fabulous animals on it may symbolize the joining of the two lands, so it is often read as a picture of Egypt's unification. It stands about 64 centimeters tall and is kept in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

title: A Script Nobody Can Read Yet
text: Accountants in Susa and across the Iranian plateau pressed signs into clay tablets in their own writing system, now called Proto-Elamite. About 1,700 tablets survive, mostly records counting farm goods, people and institutions. Yet it is one of the oldest scripts still largely undeciphered, so we can read the numbers but not most of the words.

source.name: Cambridge University Press (Cambridge Elements), 'Proto-Elamite' (2025, book abstract via Crossref)

source2.name: Penn Museum, Expedition Magazine (C. L. Hamlin, 'A Proto-Elamite Account Tablet from Susa', 1968)

title: Merneith, Egypt's First Woman Ruler?
text: Merneith was buried at Abydos in a vast tomb complex in the royal cemetery of Egypt's earliest kings. An ancient list of rulers from the time of King Den names her as "king's mother." Historians think she may have ruled as regent while Den was a child, which would make her one of the earliest women known to have governed Egypt.

title: Wagon Herders Remix Europe's DNA
text: The Yamnaya were herders on the grasslands north of the Black Sea who lived with cattle, wagons and horses. Ancient DNA shows their descendants spread deep into Europe, and a big share of many Europeans' ancestry traces back to them. Many scholars think they also spread early Indo-European languages.

title: The Woman With a Golden Eye
text: In the 'Burnt City' of eastern Iran, archaeologists found a woman in her late twenties, buried between 2900 and 2800 BCE with what they believe is an artificial eyeball. It was made of bitumen paste and gold and once held in place with fine thread. A mark in her eye socket suggests she wore it for a long time, though some experts think it was an eyepatch.

title: Gilgamesh, the Real King of Uruk
text: Gilgamesh is the hero of a famous Mesopotamian epic, but he was probably a real king who ruled Uruk sometime in the first half of the 3rd millennium BCE; the Sumerian king list names him. Later poets made him part god, a great builder and warrior who fights the forest guardian Humbaba and loses a precious plant to a serpent.

title: Imhotep Stacks the First Pyramid
text: For King Djoser, the architect Imhotep translated earlier Egyptian building into stone, stacking six tiers into a giant staircase about 60 meters tall. It is the oldest known monument of cut stone in the world. Imhotep became so famous that later Egyptians worshipped him as a god of medicine.

title: A Father's Advice in Clay
text: In the Instructions of Shuruppak, an ancient Sumerian text, a wise father gives advice to his son. Some tips are timeless, like don't speak arrogantly to your mother. Others are delightfully practical, like don't buy a donkey that brays, and don't put your field right next to a road.

source.name: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, University of Oxford

title: Peseshet, Overseer of Healer Women
text: A false door in a tomb at Giza, uncovered in 1929–30, names a woman called Peseshet with the title 'Overseer of Healer Women'. She lived during Egypt's Old Kingdom and is a genuine ancient Egyptian woman healer. Fun twist: the 'first woman doctor' Merit Ptah, often quoted online, seems to be a 1930s mix-up based on Peseshet.

source.name: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (on Kwiecinski, J. Hist. Med. 2019)

title: A Lost Culture Found by Looters
text: Beginning in 2001, ancient cemeteries south of Jiroft in southeastern Iran were plundered, and carved chlorite stone vessels poured onto the antiquities market before archaeologists could dig. Police confiscated many pieces. Scholars link them to a thriving Bronze Age culture of the later third millennium BCE, whose style of carved stonework also turns up in Mesopotamia and around the Persian Gulf.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Jiroft iii. General Survey of Excavations'

title: From Tavern Keeper to King
text: The Sumerian King List, a long list of rulers, names exactly one woman: Kubaba (written Kug-Bau) of Kish, a tavern keeper who 'made firm the foundations of Kish' and became king. The list claims she ruled for 100 years, which is surely exaggerated, so her story has to be read with caution.

source.name: Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature, University of Oxford (Sumerian King List)

title: Ebla's Lost Palace Archive
text: In 1975, archaeologists digging at Ebla found the city's archives: more than 17,000 clay tablets and fragments, lying almost in the order they had been stored on their now-collapsed shelves. A fire had destroyed the city. The tablets include vocabularies and student exercises, showing that Ebla was a major centre of learning in the 3rd millennium BCE.

title: Sargon Builds the First Empire
text: Sargon started out as a cupbearer, the king's drink-server, in the city of Kish. He went on to conquer the cities of Sumer and beyond, often called the world's first empire. A later legend says he was set adrift as a baby in a basket on the river. His capital Akkad has never been found.

title: A Boy King's Excited Letter
text: Harkhuf, a governor from Elephantine and overseer of caravans, journeyed deep into Nubia to trade. On one trip, under King Pepi II, he brought back a Pygmy from inner Africa. The young king was so delighted that he sent Harkhuf a letter, and Harkhuf proudly had it copied onto the walls of his tomb.

title: The Desert Capital of the Oxus
text: Gonur Depe was a great walled city of the Oxus Civilization, a Bronze Age culture of Central Asia that few people have heard of. At its heart stood a fortified palace, supplied by clay water pipes, and skilled potters worked in the city. Some rich graves even held whole four-wheeled wagons whose wooden wheels had metal rims.

source.name: Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, exhibition wall texts 'Margiana. A Bronze Age Kingdom in Turkmenistan' (2018)

title: The Mega-Drought That Shook Empires
text: Around 2200 BCE, the climate of northern Mesopotamia turned sharply drier and windier. In northern Syria, the city of Tell Leilan was abandoned after four centuries of urban life, and its soil layers record the change. The archaeologists who dug it link this abrupt dry spell to the collapse of the Akkadian Empire, and neighbouring regions collapsed at the same time.

source.name: Science (Weiss et al. 1993, 'The genesis and collapse of third millennium north Mesopotamian civilization')

title: An Indus Port and Its Bead Shops
text: Lothal was an Indus port town near the coast of Gujarat. Its huge walled basin, 217 meters long, has been identified as a tidal dockyard where boats sailed in at high tide. Lothal also had a bead-making factory, and finds linked to the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia show how far its trade reached.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Tentative List: Archaeological remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal

title: The Oldest Law Code We Have
text: Long before the famous Code of Hammurabi, King Ur-Nammu of Ur, or perhaps his son Shulgi, issued a set of laws. It is the oldest law code yet discovered. Dating from the middle of the 21st century BCE, it dealt with matters such as bodily injuries, runaway slaves and witchcraft.

title: A Stone Age Sunrise Calendar
text: At Taosi, a large walled town of the late Neolithic, archaeologists found a half-circle of rammed earth whose curved wall is cut by twelve gaps. Seen from a central point, two of the gaps lined up with sunrise on the summer and winter solstices around 2100 BCE. Many see it as one of China's earliest observatories, used to track the seasons.

source.name: Science in China Series G 52 (2009), Wu, Chen & Liu, 'Astronomical function and date of the Taosi observatory' (abstract, Springer)

source2.name: Springer Handbook of Archaeoastronomy and Ethnoastronomy (2015), X. Sun, 'Taosi Observatory' (abstract)

title: The First Spoked-Wheel Chariots
text: On the steppe east of the Ural Mountains, people of the Sintashta culture placed light, two-wheeled vehicles with spoked wheels in their graves around 2000 BCE. Pulled by teams of horses and built to carry people rather than goods, they are the earliest evidence of such chariots in the region. Before this, heavy wagons with solid disc wheels were pulled by cattle.

title: The World's Oldest Noodles
text: At Lajia in northwestern China, archaeologists found a sealed earthenware bowl with long, thin noodles still inside, about 4,000 years old. They were made from millet, not wheat. People still argue over whether the Chinese, Italians or Arabs invented noodles first, but these show the craft was already known here 4,000 years ago.

source.name: Nature (Lu et al. 2005, 'Millet noodles in Late Neolithic China')

title: Dilmun, Island of Merchants
text: Dilmun, on today's Bahrain, was a trading hub between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, shipping copper, pearls and dates. Between about 2200 and 1750 BCE its people built some 11,700 burial mounds, the grandest of them two-storey royal towers at A'ali. A Sumerian myth even called Dilmun a pure, pristine land without sickness.

title: The Minoans Build Knossos
text: On Crete, the Minoans built their first palace at Knossos, a group of buildings around a rectangular courtyard. The later palace had long storerooms for grain and oil, and colorful wall paintings of dolphins and bull-leaping. Ancient writers placed the mythical Labyrinth near Knossos, and some think the palace itself was meant.

title: The Temple of the Crossed Hands
text: High in the Andes near today's Huánuco, people built small temples at Kotosh around 2000–1800 BCE, at the very end of the time before pottery. One temple wall carries mud reliefs of crossed hands, giving it its nickname. Later temples were built right on top of the older ones.

title: Letters From Assyrian Traders
text: From about the 20th to the 18th century BCE, merchants from Assyria lived in a trading quarter at Kanesh in Anatolia, the end station for caravans from home. They traded Assyrian textiles for Anatolian copper and silver. Thousands of their clay tablets survive, the earliest historical documents found in Anatolia.

title: West Africa's Early Village Farmers
text: In the second millennium BCE, perhaps pushed south as the Sahara and Sahel dried, the Kintampo people settled across today's Ghana. They built wattle-and-daub structures, kept sheep or goats, and grew cowpea, pearl millet and oil palm while still foraging. They also left stone arm bands, beads and, at some sites, clay figurines.

source.name: Nyame Akuma (Society of Africanist Archaeologists), no. 48, 1997: Casey et al., 'Report of Investigations at the Birimi Site in Northern Ghana'

source2.name: Antiquity (Cambridge University Press): D'Andrea et al., 'Early domesticated cowpea from central Ghana'

title: A Medical Papyrus for Women
text: Found by Flinders Petrie in 1889 in the town of Lahun, beside the pyramid of King Senusret II, the Kahun Papyrus is one of the oldest Egyptian healing texts. It deals with women's health, listing a woman's symptoms, the healer's diagnosis and the treatment. It dates to the late Twelfth or early Thirteenth Dynasty, almost 4,000 years ago.

source.name: UCL Petrie Museum, Digital Egypt for Universities: Kahun Medical Papyrus (UC 32057)

source2.name: UCL Digital Egypt for Universities: Lahun Papyri

title: Pythagoras, a Thousand Years Early
text: A small clay tablet from Babylonia, now called Plimpton 322 and kept at Columbia University, holds a table of numbers in four columns and 15 rows. In 1945 Neugebauer and Sachs showed that it lists Pythagorean triples, whole numbers that fit the sides of right triangles. Babylonian scribes knew this over a thousand years before Pythagoras.

source.name: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

title: A Dragon Made of Turquoise
text: Erlitou, in central China, had palaces and a bronze foundry, and many scholars link it to the legendary Xia dynasty. In a noble's grave in the palace area, a 70-centimeter dragon made of more than 2,000 tiny turquoise pieces lay on the body, between shoulder and hip. It is one of the earliest dragon images in China.

source.name: Journal of Gems & Gemmology 26(5) 2024, Li Cunxin, 'Study on Archaeological Cleaning and Restoration of Turquoise-Inlaid Dragon-Shaped Artifact from Erlitou Site' (abstract; China University of Geosciences)

source2.name: China.org.cn (China Internet Information Center), 'Archaeologists Find Oldest Chinese Dragon Totem', quoting CASS Institute of Archaeology researchers Du Jinpeng and Xu Hong

title: The Mystery Disc of Phaistos
text: In 1908, the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier found a clay disc in the palace of Phaistos on Crete, covered on both sides in a spiral of 241 signs showing people, birds, plants and ships. The signs were pressed into the wet clay with tiny seals, a bit like early printing. Despite many attempts, nobody has convincingly read this one-of-a-kind object.

title: The Oldest Known Mesoamerican Ballcourt
text: Near the Pacific coast of Chiapas, villagers built an earthen court about 80 meters long for the Mesoamerican ballgame, the oldest known by some 500 years. The game was played with a rubber ball. Mesoamericans were making rubber by 1600 BCE, mixing latex with juice from a morning glory vine to make it tough and workable.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine (Archaeological Institute of America), 'Oldest Ballcourt', 1998

source2.name: MIT News: 'Rubber processed in ancient Mesoamerica, MIT researchers find'

title: Shang Walls of Pounded Earth
text: Around 1600 BCE, early Shang rulers built a city at Zhengzhou ringed by a massive wall enclosing about 3.2 square kilometers. It was made of rammed earth and measured 36 meters wide at its base. By one estimate, it would have taken 10,000 people more than 12 years to build.

title: The Gold Mask of Mycenae
text: In 1876, Heinrich Schliemann dug up royal graves at Mycenae and found a gold face mask, which he hoped belonged to Agamemnon of Trojan War fame. The mask is actually around 300 years too old for that. It still shows how rich Greece's first warrior kings had become.

title: Rice Fields in Bronze Age Korea
text: Between about 3,500 and 3,000 years ago Korea entered the Bronze Age Mumun period, and intensive farming finally took hold. Villagers grew more rice, along with wheat, soybeans, red beans and hemp, and laid out ridged dry fields and paddy fields in the south. Within about 500 years, paddy farming and bronze reached Japan.

title: Linear B: Greek's Oldest Records
text: After Mycenaeans took over Knossos, scribes there wrote clay tablets in a script called Linear B. In 1952, Michael Ventris, an architect who had loved codes since boyhood, showed it was the oldest known form of Greek. The thrilling secret texts? Detailed administrative records, used only for running the palace economy.

title: The Rigveda: Hymns Kept by Memory
text: In the Punjab region of today's India and Pakistan, poets composed the Rigveda, about a thousand hymns to gods such as Agni, the sacred fire, and the warlike Indra. For well over a thousand years it was passed on by memory, not writing, guarded by families of priests. It is the oldest of Hinduism's sacred books.

title: The Egtved Girl's Summer Burial
text: A girl of 16 to 18 was buried in an oak coffin one summer's day in 1370 BCE, wearing a short tunic, a knee-length corded skirt and a bronze belt plate decorated with spirals. Her hair, teeth, nails and clothes survived. At her feet stood a small bark bucket that had once held a kind of beer.

title: Akhenaten's City of the Sun
text: Pharaoh Akhenaten broke with tradition, devoting himself to the sun disc, the Aten, and building a brand-new capital on an empty site beside the Nile. Art changed too: house shrines showed the king in the affectionate embrace of his family. About four years after his death the city was abandoned, leaving behind portrait busts of Queen Nefertiti.

title: Tutankhamun's Dagger From Space
text: Wrapped in the linen around young King Tutankhamun's mummy was a dagger with a golden hilt, a rock crystal pommel and an iron blade. In 2016, scientists found that the blade holds lots of nickel and cobalt, so its iron came from a meteorite. Egypt did not yet smelt its own iron, so 'iron from the sky' was a treasure fit for a pharaoh.

source2.name: Eos (American Geophysical Union), E. Deatrick, 'Pharaoh's Iron Dagger Made from a Meteorite, Study Confirms' (1 June 2016)

title: Elam's Great Ziggurat
text: King Untash-Napirisha of Elam founded a holy city with a giant stepped temple tower, a ziggurat. Many of its baked bricks carry cuneiform writing naming Elam's gods. It is the best-preserved ziggurat anywhere and the largest outside Mesopotamia, even though the city around it was never finished.

title: Ramesses Carves a Mountain in Nubia
text: Ramesses II had two temples cut into a cliff in Nubia, with four giant seated statues of himself out front. Twice a year, the sunrise shines deep inside to light up statues in the back room. In the 1960s, the whole temple was cut into blocks and moved uphill to escape a dam's rising lake.

title: A Bronze Age Battlefield
text: Chance finds of weapons, horse bones and human skeletons along the banks of the River Tollense led archaeologists to the remains of a Bronze Age battle. The fighters used arrows and wooden clubs, and some came with horses. Wounds on the bones show vicious face-to-face combat, a fight missing from any written record.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge University Press): Jantzen et al. 2011, 'A Bronze Age battlefield? Weapons and trauma in the Tollense Valley, north-eastern Germany'

title: The Fall of Ugarit
text: The trading city of Ugarit on the Syrian coast, with its palaces, temples and libraries, flourished from about 1450 BCE. Then, around 1200 BCE, it fell. Its end coincided with invasions by raiders known as the Sea Peoples, and with earthquakes and famines, part of a wave of troubles across the eastern Mediterranean.

title: The First Recorded Strike
text: The skilled craftsmen who carved royal tombs lived in their own village and were paid in grain. Under Ramesses III, their rations came late again and again. So they put down their tools and sat in protest outside temples, until officials delivered. It is the first workers' strike in recorded history.

title: Questions Burned Into Turtle Shells
text: Shang kings asked about harvests, wars and even toothaches by heating turtle shells and cattle bones until they cracked. The question was written on the bone, and the shape of the crack gave the answer. Found at Anyang, the last Shang capital, these oracle bones carry the earliest known writing in China, and they name the kings who ruled there.

source.name: Asian Art Museum of San Francisco, Education, 'An Introduction to the Shang Dynasty (approx. 1500–1050 BCE)'

title: Grey Pots of the Vedic Heartland
text: Across the upper Ganges plains, people made a grey pottery now called Painted Grey Ware. Archaeologists recognised it as a culture after digs at Hastinapura in 1950-51, and date it from about 1100 BCE, in the Iron Age. Later Vedic texts place the powerful Kuru clan in this same region, where iron technology helped farming villages settle along the rivers.

source.name: INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala (UGC, Government of India): Iron Age - Antiquity of Iron in India

title: The Alphabet Goes Viral
text: Phoenician scribes used just 22 letters, all consonants, instead of hundreds of signs. Phoenician sailors carried the alphabet across the Mediterranean, and the Greeks borrowed it and added vowels. Our letter A began as a sign for 'ox', and if you flip it upside down, you can still see the horns.

title: The Zhou Win the Mandate of Heaven
text: King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at the Battle of Muye, around 1046 BCE. The Zhou taught that Heaven gave a ruler the right to rule, and would take it away if he became tyrannical. This idea, the Mandate of Heaven, was later used by Chinese historians to explain why each dynasty fell and another took its place.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tianming' (Mandate of Heaven), revised by Matt Stefon

title: The Giant Maya Platform Seen by Laser
text: Early Maya people built a flat artificial plateau about 1,400 meters long, the oldest and largest Maya monument found so far. It is so long and low that from the ground you cannot tell it is there. Its discovery was announced in 2020, after lidar, laser scans taken from aircraft, revealed its shape.

title: The Goggle-Eyed Figures of Jōmon
text: Late Jōmon people in northern Japan shaped clay figures called dogū. The most famous one, found at Tsugaru in Aomori and now in the Tokyo National Museum, has huge eyes that look like goggles, a contorted body and patterns all over. The museum dates it to between 1000 and 400 BCE and lists it as an Important Cultural Property.

dateLabel: Under way by 1000 BCE (began about 4000-2000 BCE)
title: Bantu Farmers on the Move
text: From the borderlands of today's Cameroon and Nigeria, Bantu-speaking peoples began spreading across Africa between 4,000 and 6,000 years ago, the most dramatic population movement in the continent's recent past. Over many centuries it reshaped Africa's languages and cultures. That's why some 500 related languages, from Zulu to Swahili, are spoken today.

title: Chavín's Temple of Sound
text: High in the Andes, the temple of Chavín was a pilgrimage center with a maze of stone galleries inside, complete with vents and drains. Among its carvings is a great stone called the Lanzón. Researchers studying the site's acoustics work with its conch-shell trumpets, called pututus, which may once have filled the galleries with sound.

source2.name: Stanford University CCRMA, Chavín de Huántar Archaeological Acoustics Project

title: A Party for 69,574 Guests
text: To open his new capital at Kalhu (Nimrud), Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II threw a ten-day feast for 69,574 people, according to a stone stela he set up outside his throne room. The inscription says the guests were wined and dined, then sent home 'in peace and joy'. Easily one of history's biggest parties.

source.name: Oracc 'Nimrud: Materialities of Assyrian Knowledge Production' (University of Pennsylvania Museum / UK AHRC project)

title: Polynesia's First Beach Village
text: Lapita sailors, famous for their decorated pottery, reached Tonga and settled Nukuleka about 2,800 years ago. Archaeologists identify it as a founder colony for the first settlement of Polynesia, dated very precisely from coral tools left at the site. The village has been lived in continuously ever since, beside a lagoon that is good for fishing.

title: A Steppe Chief and His Many Horses
text: In the Tuva mountains of Siberia, early Scythian-style nomads built a huge burial mound with wooden log chambers arranged like spokes of a wheel. Around a chief and his companions they buried well over a hundred horses. It is one of the oldest known tombs of the horse-riding nomads of the steppe.

source.name: Antiquity (2024), Caspari et al., 'A spectral cavalcade: Early Iron Age horse sacrifice at a royal tomb in southern Siberia' (Cambridge Core, open access)

source2.name: Sensors 19 (2019), Caspari et al., early nomadic funerary architecture in the 'Siberian Valley of the Kings' (PMC)

title: La Venta's Buried Mosaics
text: Between about 800 and 400 BCE La Venta was the leading Olmec center, with a 30-meter clay mound on what was then an island in the Tonalá River. The Olmec laid three huge mosaic pavements here, each showing a jaguar mask, and deliberately buried them soon after they were finished. Their gift was not meant for human eyes.

title: Yerevan's Ancient Fortress
text: Armenia's capital, Yerevan, traces its history back to the fortress of Erebuni, founded in the 780s BCE. Archaeology shows that people had already lived on the spot for thousands of years. The city grew into an important center of trade and has survived a long history of sieges and conquerors, from Romans and Arabs to Mongols and Persians.

title: The Great Dam of Sheba
text: At Maʾrib, capital of the kingdom of Saba, which is often linked with the Queen of Sheba, engineers built a great dam about 580 meters long, with sluice gates to control the water. Its canals turned dry land into a huge oasis that fed the region for centuries. Its final collapse, long after, is even remembered in the Quran.

dateLabel: Second half of the 8th century BCE
title: A Cheeky Poem on a Drinking Cup
text: Greek settlers on the island of Ischia scratched a short verse onto a clay drinking cup, one of the earliest surviving examples of written Greek. It says, roughly, 'I am Nestor's cup, good to drink from', and promises that whoever drains it will at once be seized by desire for Aphrodite, goddess of love.

title: Guan Zhong Makes Salt Pay
text: When Duke Huan became ruler of Qi in 685 BCE, he made Guan Zhong his chief adviser, even though Guan had backed his rival for the throne. Together they brought in a uniform tax system, a central army, and state monopolies on salt and iron. Qi became the leading power of the Spring and Autumn period, heading a league of states from 651 BCE.

title: A King Who Collected Books
text: Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, who could read Sumerian and obscure Akkadian scripts, gathered a great library of clay tablets at Nineveh: omens, prayers, science and stories. More than 20,000 tablets and fragments survive in the British Museum, even though enemies sacked the city in 612 BCE. Thanks to the library, we can still read the Epic of Gilgamesh.

title: The First Coins Have a Lion
text: The kingdom of Lydia began stamping small lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver panned from its rivers, with designs such as a lion's head. Ancient Greek writers credited the Lydians with inventing coinage, and the coins themselves back them up. Later the Lydian king Croesus introduced the first coins of pure gold.

source.name: Archaeological Exploration of Sardis (Harvard Art Museums / Cornell): J. H. Kroll, 'The Coins of Sardis'

title: Sappho Sings of Love
text: On the island of Lesbos, Sappho wrote lyric poems admired in every age for their beauty. In antiquity she was counted among the greatest poets, and Plato is said to have hailed her as 'the tenth Muse'. Her work once filled nine books, but only one poem survives complete; the rest are fragments, many recovered from ancient papyrus since 1898.

title: An Eclipse Stops a War
text: The Lydians and Medes had been at war for five years when, in the middle of a battle, day suddenly turned to night. Herodotus says both sides stopped fighting and were eager to make peace. He also claims Thales of Miletus had foretold it, though modern scholars doubt he could have. Astronomers match it to the total eclipse of May 28, 585 BCE.

source.name: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center: Solar Eclipses of History

title: Babylon's Brilliant Blue Gate
text: King Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon with a dazzling entrance, the Ishtar Gate, covered in shiny blue glazed bricks. Rows of lions, bulls and dragons march along its walls. Archaeologists shipped its pieces to Berlin, where a reconstruction stands in a museum today.

source.name: Institute for the Study of the Ancient World, New York University

title: Laws Cast on a Bronze Cauldron
text: Zichan, chief minister of the small state of Zheng, had the state's penal laws cast in bronze for all to see. It is often described as the earliest recorded publication of written laws in China. A critic, Shuxiang, warned that once people knew the rules they would appeal to the written word, and lawsuits and bribery would multiply.

source.name: University of Hong Kong, Department of Philosophy (Chad Hansen)

title: Nok Sculptors and Iron Smelters
text: In central Nigeria, the Nok people made striking clay sculptures of people with fancy hairstyles and large triangular eyes with pierced pupils. Around this time they were also smelting iron, among the earliest in West Africa. The first Nok sculpture turned up in a tin mine near the village of Nok in 1928.

title: Ethiopia's Ancient Stone Temple
text: In the highlands of Tigray, builders in the kingdom of D'mt raised a tall temple of perfectly fitted stone blocks, laid without mortar. Its style closely copies temples of Saba across the Red Sea in Yemen. Still standing, roofless, after about 2,700 years, it is the oldest standing building in Ethiopia.

source.name: ISPRS Archives XXXVIII-5/W16 (2011), Lindstaedt, Mechelke, Schnelle & Kersten (German Archaeological Institute / HafenCity University), 'Virtual reconstruction of the Almaqah Temple of Yeha in Ethiopia'
